nameStory: The downy jumping spider gets its name from the fine, soft hairs that cover its body, giving it a fuzzy, downy appearance like a baby bird's first feathers. This velvety coating helps distinguish it from its smoother jumping spider cousins. The scientific name 'pubescens' comes from Latin meaning 'becoming hairy,' referring to this same downy characteristic.
description: The downy jumping spider is a small, compact arachnid with the characteristic stocky build and large front-facing eyes of all jumping spiders. These tiny hunters typically measure about 4-6mm in length, roughly the size of a pencil eraser. Their bodies are covered in dense, fine hairs that give them a soft, fuzzy texture, and they're usually brownish or grayish with subtle markings. Like all jumping spiders, they're active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch it.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rectangular body that feels firm and substantial despite its small size, with a distinctly fuzzy texture from dense fine hairs

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a row, with the middle pair noticeably larger and more prominent, giving an alert, almost curious expression

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Subtle brownish or grayish coloration with faint patterns that can vary, but always overlaid with the characteristic downy hair coating

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small at 4-6mm long, about the size of a pencil eraser or small ladybug

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops to look around, often turning to face you directly when approached

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small silk retreats or shelters rather than catching webs, usually found as tiny silk-lined spaces under bark or in crevices

habitat: Downy jumping spiders prefer sun-warmed surfaces like tree bark, wooden fences, rock walls, and building exteriors throughout New England. They're often found on oak, maple, and pine trees, hunting for small insects in the textured bark crevices. Look for them on south-facing surfaces that get good morning sun, from sea level up to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter shelters and become active on warm, sunny days, often seen basking on tree bark and wooden surfaces in late morning.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during the day, and mating displays can be observed with males performing courtship dances.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with females creating silk egg sacs in protected locations before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in silk-lined retreats under loose bark, in rock crevices, or other protected spots, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Downy jumping spiders can see in color and have vision that's sharper than many birds - they can spot a moving insect from over 20 times their own body length away, which would be like a human clearly seeing a basketball from over 100 feet away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the downy jumping spider's fuzzy, hair-covered appearance sets it apart from the smoother, shinier bold jumping spider and other common species. Memory trick: if it looks like it needs a tiny hairbrush, it's probably a downy jumping spider!
contextualKnowledge: This species was reclassified in 2017 from the genus Sitticus to Attulus, so older field guides and websites may still list it as Sitticus pubescens. This type of reclassification is common in spider taxonomy as DNA analysis reveals new relationships between species.
compareHints: Among its Attulus relatives in New England, the downy jumping spider is distinguished by its particularly dense hair coating compared to the Asiatic wall jumping spider, which has a smoother appearance. The flower jumping spider tends to be found more often on flowers and has different markings, while the downy prefers bark and wooden surfaces. All share the same basic jumping spider body plan but differ in their preferred microhabitats and surface textures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives in the Attulus genus, the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider is more associated with artificial structures rather than natural habitats.
The Flower Jumping Spider is smaller and more flower-focused than its relatives like the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider, which prefers vertical surfaces like walls and tree trunks.
Compared to its relatives like the Asiatic Wall Jumping Spider, this species appears to prefer sandy habitats rather than human structures.
